Contributing an atlas package

Source: vignettes/contributing.Rmd
contributing.Rmd

ggseg atlases live in their own R packages, distributed through the ggsegverse r-universe. This gives users a single place to install from, whether your package is hosted on GitHub, GitLab or elsewhere.

This article covers the last step: getting a finished atlas package listed on r-universe. For building the package itself — scaffolding it with setup_atlas_repo(), writing the data-raw/ build script, documenting the atlas, and getting R CMD check to pass — see Publishing an atlas, which walks through a complete example.

What we expect of a package

  1. The atlas works with ggseg, ggseg3d, or both.
  2. It lives in its own R package.
  3. That package is in a public version control repository.
  4. It passes R CMD check without errors.

setup_atlas_repo() gives you a package that satisfies all four from the start, including tests, GitHub Actions workflows and a pkgdown site. In RStudio it is also available from the New Project dialog, under the ggseg icon.

The core table

Every atlas carries a core table, one row per region. Four columns have a fixed meaning across the whole ecosystem, and anything else is yours.

Column Required What it holds
label yes the identifier, unique within the atlas
region yes a short, readable key
hemi yes "left", "right", "midline", or NA
display expected the long-form name, for legends and axes

The pipelines fill all four in, so a generated atlas satisfies this without you doing anything. The guidance below matters when you curate the result, which most atlases need.

label is the join key

label is what the palette and every geometry slot are keyed on, so it has to be unique and it has to stay put. Rename it and the geometry decouples from the metadata, which draws a region in the wrong colour, or not at all. If you do need to re-key, ggseg.formats::relabel_atlas() rewrites all of them together.

Keep the source parcellation’s spelling here, even when it is ugly. A reader tracing your atlas back to its publication needs that string.

region is the key people type

region is the short form a user writes in their own results table, so it should be the readable version of label: no hemisphere, no suffix that is the same on every row. lh_L_V1_ROI becomes v1 roi; Left-Thalamus becomes thalamus.

The pipelines derive it with label_to_region(), which strips the hemisphere and normalises separators and case. It is a reasonable default, not a rule — it cannot know that ROI carries nothing or that V1 should keep its capitals. Where it gets your atlas wrong, declare a region column in your lookup table and it is used exactly as you wrote it.

Two things to get right, because nothing can check them for you:

  • Do not leave the hemisphere in region. If region is unique across the whole atlas when the parcellation is bilateral, the hemisphere is almost certainly still in there, and grouping by region then silently aggregates nothing.
  • Unless there genuinely is no pair. Data-driven parcellations often number parcels globally, so a left parcel has no right counterpart to share a name with. Then region being unique is correct, and forcing a shared name would invent an anatomical claim the parcellation does not make. Say which situation yours is in, in the atlas’s documentation.

hemi is a closed vocabulary

hemi takes "left", "right", "midline" or NA, and nothing else is accepted. It is the one column with no room for per-atlas judgement, because plots filter and facet on it: a fifth spelling does not raise an error, it drops those rows from the figure.

NA is for structures where a side does not apply. Use it rather than inventing a value, and do not leave it NA for only part of an atlas — that is the case that bites, since hemi == "left" quietly loses rows.

A finer distinction than side belongs in a column of your own. The cerebellar vermis is recorded as "midline", for instance; if you need to pick the vermis out, add a column that says so.

display is for people

display is the long-form name, spelled to read well in a legend: region "bankssts" has display "banks of superior temporal sulcus". It is what lets region stay terse without the figure becoming unreadable.

If you leave it out you get a message once per session telling you so. It is not an error, because about twenty atlas packages were published before the column existed, but a plot of your atlas has nothing but the machine key to put in its legend.

Everything else is yours

Add whatever columns classify your atlas usefully — the bundled atlases use lobe, structure, group and label_short — and nothing constrains their names or contents. They survive the atlas verbs and reach the user’s data frame, so a column like network or lobe is immediately available to facet or colour by.

Adding your package to r-universe

1. Fork the r-universe repository

Fork ggsegverse/ggsegverse.r-universe.dev.

2. Add yourself to packages.json

packages.json lists every package in the ggsegverse r-universe. Add an entry for yours:

[
  {
    "package": "ggsegYeo2011",
    "url": "https://github.com/ggsegverse/ggsegYeo2011"
  },
  {
    "package": "yourpackage",
    "url": "https://github.com/yourusername/yourpackage"
  }
]

package must match the Package field of your DESCRIPTION exactly, and url points at the repository. For a repository that is not on GitHub, or one whose default branch is not the one to build, add branch:

{
  "package": "yourpackage",
  "url": "https://gitlab.com/yourusername/yourpackage",
  "branch": "main"
}

3. Open a pull request

Include a sentence on what the atlas is and a link to the paper it comes from, if there is one.

4. Review

We check that the package installs, that it passes R CMD check, and that the atlas plots with ggseg and/or ggseg3d. Once merged, r-universe builds it automatically and it appears at ggsegverse.r-universe.dev, usually within the hour.

Once you are listed

Users install your atlas with:

install.packages(
  "yourpackage",
  repos = "https://ggsegverse.r-universe.dev"
)

r-universe rebuilds on every push to your repository, so updates need nothing from you. If you move the repository, open another pull request to update its url in packages.json.
